A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same OENN/CENN research and contain readable text, equations, tables, and Appendices A–B. Matching content across page reflow establishes that the main architecture, universality results, and proofs are retained.

before.justification: Appendix A.3 states that the authors compared GrothendieckCENN with TemporalCNN and InvariantTransformer on EMG-IMU. Table 2 reports accuracy and F1 outcomes without identifying them as reproduced results from another paper.

after.justification: Appendix A explicitly describes the experimental applications as a review of related literature, and A.3 and Table 2 attribute the CatHAR results to Maruyama and Yasuda (2026). Despite the phrase 'we evaluate,' no separate original empirical outcomes are identified.

M1.justification: The general OENN architecture is unchanged. The Appendix A.3 application changes its symmetry construction from ACC/GYR/EMG fusion with temporal and electrode shifts to sensor-configuration coarsening with independent SO(3) frames. This is a specific adaptation; the newly documented classifier pipeline does not establish revisions to the retained general method.

E1.justification: Appendix A.3 replaces EMG-IMU multimodal action/gesture classification with CatHAR, a controlled six-class activity-recognition benchmark using five IMUs and subject-dependent sensor frames. Removing EMG and introducing a task designed around cross-sensor rotational geometry materially changes the represented data and evaluation scenario.

E2.justification: Table 2 replaces the names TemporalCNN and InvariantTransformer with CNN and Transformer alongside the benchmark replacement. V1 provides insufficient baseline descriptions to determine whether these are different implementations or renamed versions. V2's description of untransported baseline inputs does not fully resolve that correspondence.

E3.justification: V2 introduces a specified CatHAR evaluation protocol: 1080 length-96 sequences, 18 subjects, a 12/3/3 subject-wise training/validation/test split, and training and reported testing on the fine five-sensor configuration. Accuracy and explicitly identified macro-F1 replace the sparsely specified EMG-IMU evaluation. These are settings for a replacement study, not demonstrated changes to a retained experiment.

E4.justification: Neither version reports ablations, sensitivity analyses, or separate robustness results. V2 mentions a coarse-configuration consistency evaluation in the cited paper but supplies no corresponding outcomes. The replacement benchmark table and its explanatory discussion do not constitute an added supplementary analysis.

E5.justification: V2 identifies Table 2 values as means over five independent runs; v1 supplies no run count or averaging statement. This adds repeated-run reporting without establishing an increase in runs for a retained experiment. Neither version provides dispersion estimates, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: Table 2 replaces all empirical entries. V1 reports accuracy/F1 of 0.428/0.399, 0.646/0.592, and 0.904/0.903 for TemporalCNN, InvariantTransformer, and GrothendieckCENN on EMG-IMU. V2 reports mean accuracy/macro-F1 of 0.493/0.467, 0.633/0.582, and 0.978/0.978 for CNN, Transformer, and GrothendieckCENN on CatHAR. GrothendieckCENN remains first, but these are different-setting results rather than demonstrated performance gains.

T1.justification: Appendix A.3 replaces the modality-fusion group assignments with formal sensor-configuration surjections, coarsening morphisms, SO(3) product groups, and their pullback maps. It also states the predictor's configuration-naturality equation. The general CENN definitions, OENN theorems, embedding results, and Appendix B proofs are unchanged.

C1.justification: The abstract removes the explicit assertion that no sheaf-network UAT was previously known, while retaining the claim of new sheaf-network results. It also describes the CENN contribution as clarifying relationships rather than presenting an additional general-UAT extension. The principal OENN contributions in the introduction and conclusion remain unchanged.

C2.justification: V1 explains performance through general resistance to pose, temporal-shift, and electrode-placement nuisances. V2 gives a task-specific interpretation: three CatHAR classes share magnitude/frequency statistics but differ in relational geometry, and GrothendieckCENN uses relative rotations that the baselines do not explicitly incorporate. This makes the explanation and its applicability more specific; the theoretical limitations are unchanged.

D1.justification: V2 documents torso-frame alignment, multiplicity-aware pushforward, invariant channels built from norms and scalar products, and a patch-based Transformer followed by an MLP. It adds dataset and split details but leaves the full protocol to the cited paper. The former EMG-IMU data references disappear; neither version supplies code or a complete training recipe.

R1.justification: V2 removes the two Khan et al. dataset references associated with EMG-IMU and explicitly positions the appendix experiments as reviewed applications from prior work, including direct attribution of Table 2 to Maruyama and Yasuda (2026). The broader related-work discussion and OENN/CENN positioning remain largely intact.

P1.justification: The abstract is rewritten, the Appendix A introduction is clarified, and A.3 is retitled and substantially rewritten around human activity recognition instead of multimodal learning. These edits are localized; the main section organization and most mathematical exposition are unchanged.

P2.justification: Table 1 gains a source citation in its caption. Table 2 receives a new benchmark, averaging, and source caption, shorter labels, and adjusted column widths. References and nearby appendix text reflow, but both tables retain their basic structures and no figures or additional tables are introduced.

improvement.justification: V2 improves the appendix's transparency by explicitly attributing the reported results and documenting the subject split, averaging practice, feature construction, and differing use of relative rotations. These details make the example easier to assess. The replacement sacrifices the earlier multimodal example, and its higher scores do not demonstrate a comparable performance gain. With the main theory and proofs unchanged, the overall benefit is limited to clearer attribution, documentation, and interpretation.
